notable_absence.predicate: belongsToIndexClass / isSubtypeOf / providesIndexType / (unfilled) index maintenance model
notable_absence.finding: The registry has NO SUBSUMPTION VOCABULARY. 195 concepts, 64 predicates, and not one broader/narrower/isA relation - so a page whose entire content is a two-level taxonomy could not be expressed at all without minting. That is the deepest structural finding of the batch: nine rounds of reference extraction produced a flat vocabulary because reference pages enumerate siblings (clauses of a statement, values of a setting) and never state hierarchy. I minted two predicates rather than one, because the page draws two genuinely different hierarchical relations and uses different words for them: 'classes' (belongsToIndexClass, the Traditional/Vector split it declares up front) and a plain identity statement that one type IS another with a restriction ('Composite Vector Indexes ... which are Global Secondary Indexes (GSIs) with a single vector column' - isSubtypeOf). Reconciliation may want to generalize both to skos:broader; I did not, because the two are not interchangeable and collapsing them would erase the finding that the class axis and the type axis OVERLAP rather than nest. A FOURTH AXIS I COULD NOT MODEL AND AM REPORTING INSTEAD: index maintenance/freshness. 'Couchbase Server maintains every primary index asynchronously' and 'When operational data changes, Couchbase Server updates analytics indexes automatically' are two statements about how current an index is kept, on two different index types, on one page. The registry's nearest concept is n1ql:scan-consistency, but that is a per-QUERY setting about how current a scan must be, not a per-INDEX-TYPE property of how the index is maintained. I minted nothing for this and asserted no relation, because a two-member ad hoc scheme built from two adverbs ('asynchronously', 'automatically') would be inventing a vocabulary the docs do not have. Recording it as an absence instead. RELATION DELIBERATELY OMITTED: I did not assert tradesOffAgainst between index-type:hyperscale-vector and index-type:composite-vector, even though that predicate exists in the registry with recurrence 10 and was minted for exactly that pair. This page describes each one's strengths in separate entries and never compares them, so the comparison would have been my inference, not the page's statement.

cross_component_finding: (1) DIRECT CONTRADICTION with services.md, one directory away. This page: 'The [Search](../services/search-service.md) and [Analytics Services](../services/analytics-service.md) create and use their own indexes', and 'The [Analytics Service](../services/analytics-service.md) provides analytics indexes'. services.md: 'Index Service: Creates indexes, for use by the Query and Analytics services.' These cannot both be true. Both relations are recorded, on their respective pages, so reconciliation sees the conflict rather than inheriting whichever page happened to be extracted last. This needs an SME, not a reconciler. (2) FOUR NAMESPACES, ONE LIST. The eight index kinds this page presents as one flat enumeration already live in the corpus under four different prefixes: index-type:* (primary, secondary, gsi, hyperscale-vector, composite-vector), search:* (full-text-index), vector-index:* (search-vector-index), index:* (view). I reused every one of them rather than mint a clean parallel set, so this record deliberately contains the incoherence instead of hiding it behind eight new ids. The fix is a reconciliation decision; the evidence for it is this page, which proves the docs treat all eight as one kind of thing. (3) The Views entry is the only one with no providesIndexType relation, because Views are the only index kind on the page not provided by a service - they are produced by a deprecated engine the page does not name. An ontology that assumes every index has a providing service will have a hole exactly here. (4) SNAPSHOT ARTIFACT: the Analytics link target is written '7%5Fusing%5Findex.md' - underscores percent-encoded - which will not resolve as a filesystem path. Likely a Markdown-conversion bug affecting any docs path containing underscores, not just this one.
cross_product_finding: ANSWER TO THE INDEX-TAXONOMY QUESTION THIS BATCH WAS SET. The two canonical conceptual pages distinguish exactly FIVE axes, and use distinct words for four of them. (a) CLASS - the page's own word: 'two classes of indexes', Traditional vs Vector. (b) TYPE - the page's own word: 'the following types of indexes', eight members. (c) PROVIDING SERVICE - Index / Search / Analytics, the organising principle of every entry, and the axis the registry's service:* family already covers. (d) STORAGE MODE - index-service.md's word 'storage': standard vs memory-optimized, a property of the SERVICE's configuration and edition-gated, not a property of an index. (e) The SERVICE AS DEPLOYABLE COMPONENT - services.md's Index Service with its wire identifier 'index', its memory quota, its 8.0 on-demand add/remove, its Supervisor and its Projector and Router. Critically, classes and types do NOT nest cleanly: a Composite Vector Index is stated to BE a GSI, so index-class:vector overlaps index-type:gsi, and a Search index is classed Traditional while a Search Vector index is classed Vector - the class axis cuts across the service axis. AND WHAT THE CONCEPTUAL PAGES DO NOT DISTINGUISH AT ALL: index STATE. Neither page mentions an index lifecycle, a DDL state, warmup, pause, or readiness. The registry's index-state scheme (scheduled for creation/deferred/building/pending/online/offline/abridged) and capella:index-ui-status (ready/pause/warmup) have no conceptual-documentation basis whatsoever - they are artifacts of the SQL++ statement reference and the Capella console respectively. So of the four axes the brief suspected were conflated, the docs support three (type, service-as-component, plus class and storage mode which the brief did not list) and are SILENT on the fourth (state). That silence is a documentation gap as much as an ontology one: nothing in server/'s learn tree tells a reader that an index has a lifecycle at all.
